subject: English
description: Noun number — singular and plural forms, irregular plurals, foreign-origin plurals, collective nouns.

questions.stem: Choose the CORRECT plural form of 'criterion'.
questions.explanation: Greek-origin nouns ending in -on form plurals with -a: criterion → criteria; phenomenon → phenomena; automaton → automata. KEY RULE: words borrowed from Greek/Latin keep their original plural endings in formal English. COMMON LIST: criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena, datum → data, medium → media, bacterium → bacteria, syllabus → syllabi/syllabuses. USAGE TIP: 'data is' vs 'data are' is now a stylistic choice — formal scientific writing uses 'data are' (treating data as plural of datum); colloquial usage treats 'data' as singular mass-noun. EXAM TRAP: 'criterias' is the most common wrong answer because students apply standard '-s' plural to an already-plural form. PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC CGL, CHSL, IBPS Clerk all reuse this exact word 1-2× per paper cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing whether you've memorized the Greek/Latin plural list — a standard editor-level skill in journalism, academia, civil services drafting.

questions.stem: Which is the CORRECT plural of 'mouse' (the rodent)?
questions.explanation: VOWEL-CHANGE PLURAL (Old English umlaut pattern): mouse → mice; goose → geese; foot → feet; tooth → teeth; man → men; woman → women. INTERESTING TWIST: 'computer mouse' (the device) is plural as 'mouses' OR 'mice' depending on style guide — Oxford prefers 'mice', Microsoft style guide allows 'mouses'. ETYMOLOGY: this i-mutation reflects Proto-Germanic vowel-fronting before plural suffix; the suffix later disappeared but the vowel change stayed. EXAM TRAP: 'mooses' for moose — moose's plural is 'moose' (no change), not 'mooses' or 'meese'. RELATED IRREGULARS: child → children (-en plural), ox → oxen, brother → brethren (archaic). PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 such irregular-plural Qs every SSC CGL Tier 1 paper.

questions.explanation: Greek -is endings change to -es in plural: analysis → analyses; basis → bases; crisis → crises; thesis → theses; oasis → oases; hypothesis → hypotheses; axis → axes; parenthesis → parentheses. PRONUNCIATION DIFFERS: singular 'analysis' (-is) vs plural 'analyses' (-eez) — note the change in vowel. EXAM TRAP: 'analysises' is wrong because we don't add -es to an already-Greek-pluralized form. WRITING TIP: in essays/reports, prefer 'analyses' over 'analysis' when summarizing multiple studies — improves scholarly tone. PYQ ANGLE: this exact word appeared in CGL 2019 and 2022. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests whether you can recognize Greek-derived nouns by their -is/-on/-um endings and apply the right transformation rule.

questions.stem: Which is the CORRECT plural of 'leaf'?
questions.explanation: F → V change rule: nouns ending in -f or -fe often change to -ves in plural. Leaf → leaves; knife → knives; wife → wives; life → lives; wolf → wolves; calf → calves; half → halves; thief → thieves; loaf → loaves. EXCEPTIONS (just add -s): chief → chiefs; roof → roofs; cliff → cliffs; belief → beliefs; proof → proofs. SPECIAL CASE: 'leafs' is correct ONLY in the verb form ('she leafs through pages') or the proper noun 'Toronto Maple Leafs' (NHL team — deliberately ungrammatical name). EXAM TRAP: students hyper-correct 'roofs' to 'rooves' — wrong, 'roofs' is standard. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 -f/-ves Qs per paper cycle in SSC. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests pattern-recognition + memorization of exceptions — a classic 'rule + irregular' English structure.

questions.stem: Identify the correct plural form: A flock of ___ flew across the sky.
questions.explanation: Goose → geese: another vowel-change (umlaut) plural like foot/feet, tooth/teeth. NOTE: 'goose' meaning 'silly person' takes regular plural ('gooses' is sometimes used informally) but the BIRD always becomes 'geese'. COLLECTIVE NOUN PRACTICE: a 'flock' of geese / sheep / birds; a 'gaggle' of geese (specifically when ON THE GROUND) — geese in flight are a 'skein'. WORLD-NATURE: Bar-headed Geese famously fly OVER Mt Everest (>8,500 m altitude) — they have specialized hemoglobin for low-oxygen flight; popular CGL/UPSC GK trivia. INDIA ANGLE: India has 11 species of geese-like waterbirds; the Bar-headed Goose winters in the Sambhar/Pong Dam wetlands. EXAM TRAP: 'gooses' creeps into compound usage ('he gooses the engine') but for the BIRD always 'geese'.

questions.stem: What is the plural of the foreign-origin noun 'cactus'?
questions.explanation: Latin -us nouns typically pluralize with -i: cactus → cacti; nucleus → nuclei; alumnus → alumni; radius → radii; fungus → fungi; stimulus → stimuli; locus → loci; syllabus → syllabi (or syllabuses). NOTE: 'cactuses' IS accepted by Oxford and Webster as an alternative plural — but for SSC/IBPS exams, 'cacti' is the safer pick. EXCEPTIONS to -us → -i: 'genus' → 'genera' (Greek-style), 'corpus' → 'corpora'. EXAM TIP: when you see -us, ask 'is it Latin?' — if yes, default to -i; if uncertain, regular -es works in most modern contexts. INTERESTING: 'octopus' is GREEK origin, not Latin, so technically 'octopi' is hypercorrect — Greek would give 'octopodes'; modern usage allows 'octopuses' (most natural) or 'octopi' (semi-popular). PYQ ANGLE: 'cacti', 'fungi', 'alumni' all appear in SSC CGL across years.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses noun-number CORRECTLY? 'The news ___ coming in fast.'
questions.explanation: Despite ending in -s, NEWS is grammatically SINGULAR (an uncountable mass noun): 'the news IS encouraging'; 'no news IS good news'. Same pattern: mathematics, physics, economics, politics, statistics, civics, ethics, athletics, gymnastics — all -ics nouns are singular when referring to the SUBJECT/FIELD. BUT they can be plural when referring to ACTIVITIES/QUALITIES: 'his statistics ARE impressive' (= his data/numbers); 'her politics ARE radical' (= her political views). MEMORY TRICK — singular -s nouns: NEWS, SCIENCE-NAMES (-ics), MEASLES, MUMPS, BILLIARDS, DOMINOES. EXAM TRAP: 'the data are/is' — both accepted; formal science prefers 'data are', everyday English often uses 'data is'. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests whether you recognize that morphology (the -s) doesn't always equal plural number — mass-noun grammar is a higher-order English skill.
